title: Dawn, awake
hook: the morning star rises; he is the Buddha, the one who woke up

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three watches: past lives, beings and their deeds, and the ending of the taints. Your line was night has watches. Did a hard stretch feel lighter in parts? Day fifty-five.

Before a sunrise, there's a stretch when the sky goes from dark to not-dark, and nobody watching can say exactly when it happened. On a camping trip, after a sleepless night, from the window of an early flight, it looks the same. And some mornings, low in the east, one bright point of light hangs on after the other stars have faded. The morning star. The planet Venus. The wanderer has sat through the whole night. The third watch is ending. And the tellings, especially in East Asia, say that as the morning star rose, it was done. Today's word is what he had become.
screen: `BEFORE THE SUN.` → `DARK, THEN NOT-DARK.` → `THE MORNING STAR RISES.`

segments.voice: Buddha. It isn't a name. It's a description. It comes from the same root as bodhi, budh, to wake up. Buddha means the one who has woken up. The awakened one. The man under the tree was Siddhattha Gotama, a Sakyan, a former prince, a wanderer. At dawn, Buddhists say, he became the Buddha. There's a story in the suttas about this very word. Some time later, a brahmin named Dona sees the Buddha's footprints on a road, marked with wheels, and follows them, amazed. He finds him sitting under a tree and asks: are you a god? No, says the Buddha. A heavenly musician? No. A spirit? No. A human being? No. Then what are you? And the Buddha explains: everything that would make him any of those things has been cut off at the root, like a palm tree stump that can't grow again. Like a lotus that grows in the water and rises above it, unsoiled. So remember me, he says, as awake. Buddha. Traditions remember the day differently. Theravada Buddhists celebrate the awakening on Vesak, a full-moon day that also remembers his birth and his death. In Japan, the day of awakening is kept in December, and some Zen monasteries sit through the night before it, waiting for the morning star. Different calendars, the same dawn. And the same one word. Not a god. Not a spirit. Awake.
screen: `BUDDHA — THE ONE WHO WOKE UP.` · `ARE YOU A GOD? NO.` · `REMEMBER ME AS AWAKE.` · `VESAK, OR DECEMBER.` · then, large: `AWAKE.`

segments.voice: If there's a window, face toward the light. If not, close your eyes and picture a sunrise: the dark sky, the thin line of light in the east, one bright star still hanging there. Watch the sky change slowly, from black to deep blue to gray to gold. Don't hurry it. Let it take the whole sit. And as the light comes, notice your own awareness, the simple fact that you are awake, right now, seeing. The bell holds the time.
Buddha. The awakened one, the one who woke up, from the root budh. Not a name, but what Siddhattha became at dawn.
Your line: awake. Today, watch a sunrise or a sunset, or just the light changing through a window, and let yourself be fully awake for it. Day fifty-five.

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists celebrate the awakening on Vesak, the full moon of the month of Vesakha, and in Japan it is kept as Bodhi Day (Rohatsu) in December, in some Zen communities with meditation through the night.

fork.setup: you're Dona. you follow extraordinary footprints to a man under a tree. you ask: are you a god? a spirit? a human? what does he say?
options: I am a human, like you.
fork.reveal: he says no to each, and then: remember me as awake. Buddha. like a lotus risen above the water, unsoiled by it.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: awakened, the one who has woken up; from budh, to wake.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddha is a name, like a surname.
what it means: Buddha is a description: the awakened one. Siddhattha became it at dawn.

what a scholar hears: buddha, past participle of budh (awakened); in the Dona Sutta (AN 4.36) he refuses the categories deva, gandhabba, yakkha and human; the morning star is especially emphasized in East Asian tradition.

sources.ref: Dona Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 4.36): remember me as awake
Mahasaccaka Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 36): the awakening at the end of the third watch

notes: The morning star (Venus) at the moment of awakening: prominent in East Asian and Zen tradition (Rohatsu); the Pali sources give dawn. The script attributes it to 'the tellings, especially in East Asia'. Confirm.
AN 4.36 (Dona) paraphrased; the Buddha refuses deva, gandhabba, yakkha and manussa; the palm-stump and lotus similes. Confirm.
Vesak: Theravada tradition places birth, awakening and parinibbana on the same full moon. Bodhi Day (Rohatsu) on December 8 in Japan. Confirm 'early December'.
The script says he 'became the Buddha' at dawn; confirm this wording for all schools.
